STMPA.PA.company_overview: Franco-Italian IDM (integrated device manufacturer) that designs and fabricates a broad mix of analog, power, microcontroller, MEMS sensor and RF chips. ~80% of revenue comes from automotive and industrial customers buying microcontrollers (STM32 franchise), silicon-carbide (SiC) power devices for EV inverters, and MEMS sensors. ST owns its own fabs in France, Italy and Singapore and is co-investing with Tower and GlobalFoundries on a new 300mm fab at Crolles.

revenue_mix.segment: Analog, Power & Discrete, MEMS and Sensors (APMS — combines AM&S + P&D)
Microcontrollers, Digital ICs & RF (MDRF — combines EMP + RF&OC)

end_markets: Automotive (EV inverters via SiC, ADAS, body electronics)

moat.type: Vertically integrated SiC + STM32 microcontroller ecosystem lock-in
moat.narrative: ST is one of only two volume merchant SiC suppliers (with Wolfspeed) and supplies Tesla's main traction inverter — fab-internal SiC substrate growth at Catania/Norrkoping is a process advantage few peers can replicate. The STM32 MCU franchise has ~50,000 active customers and >1M registered developers, creating switching costs in industrial designs.

key_customers: Apple (largest customer, historically ~15-17% of revenue for image sensors)
Tesla (SiC traction inverter)
Bosch, Continental, Stellantis (auto Tier 1s and OEMs)
Mobileye/Intel (auto SoC partnerships)
key_risks: FY2025 revenue fell -11% to $11.8B with Power & Discrete (SiC) down -31% on ASP collapse — Chinese SiC entrants (Sicc, TankeBlue) plus Wolfspeed Chapter 11 disruption pressuring pricing through 2026
Apple revenue concentration: loss of MEMS/ToF socket on iPhone 17 reset cycle would create a multi-quarter air pocket
French + Italian governments together hold ~27.5% via STM Holding — limits capacity rationalisation; 2025 layoff plan triggered French union pushback and political scrutiny

SNDK.company_overview: Pure-play NAND flash memory company spun off from Western Digital on Feb 21, 2025. Designs, manufactures (via JV with Kioxia in Yokkaichi/Kitakami, Japan) and sells NAND wafers, client SSDs, enterprise SSDs, removable cards and USB drives. ~$7B revenue run-rate. The spin separated NAND from WD's hard-drive business so each could be valued on different cycle dynamics.
end_markets: AI inference servers (high-capacity TLC/QLC enterprise SSDs)
Retail consumer storage (cards, USBs under SanDisk brand)

moat.type: Joint-venture NAND fab co-investment with Kioxia + retail brand
moat.narrative: The Yokkaichi/Kitakami JV with Kioxia gives Sandisk 50% capacity claim on the world's #3-#4 NAND fab footprint at a fraction of standalone capex — replicating this from scratch would cost >$30B and 5+ years. SanDisk retains the premium consumer brand (cards, drives) that commands 20-30% retail price premium vs Samsung/Lexar.

key_customers: Hyperscalers (AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud — enterprise SSD)
PC OEMs (Dell, HP, Lenovo, Asus)
Apple, Samsung (mobile NAND)
Smartphone OEMs in China
key_risks: NAND pricing is highly cyclical — bull cycle since 2H24 driven by AI/HBM crowd-out of conventional DRAM/NAND wafer starts; supply-glut risk if Samsung/SK accelerate node migrations into 2027
Customer/JV dependency on Kioxia: any equity action by Bain/Toshiba on Kioxia (announced 2025 IPO + secondaries) reshapes Sandisk's bargaining and supply economics
Trails Samsung and SK on BiCS8/QLC enterprise SSD qualification — risk of missing the AI inference SSD design-in cycle through 2026

DOCN.company_overview: Cloud infrastructure provider targeting developers, startups and SMBs — sells compute (Droplets), managed Kubernetes, managed databases, object storage, and (since 2024 Paperspace acquisition) GPU instances and the Gradient AI platform for inference. Revenue is subscription, usage-based; FY2025 revenue $901M (+15%), hit $1B annualized monthly run-rate in Dec 2025. Pricing is typically 40-50% below AWS/Azure/GCP for equivalent compute.

moat.type: Developer-experience simplicity + price-point for SMB segment
moat.narrative: Self-serve UI, transparent flat-rate pricing and 1-click app marketplace are explicitly designed for solo developers — hyperscalers' enterprise-first console is a moat-by-neglect for DO. Switching costs are low individually but high in aggregate once an SMB has tutorials/scripts/CI tooling wired to DO APIs.

key_customers: ~640K paying customers, no >10% concentration
Million-dollar-plus ARR cohort: $133M ARR (+123% YoY in 2025)
AI cohort: $120M ARR (+150% YoY)
key_risks: AWS Lightsail / Azure Container Apps directly priced to undercut DO's SMB segment — hyperscaler $380B+ AI capex (2025) creates margin pressure across the stack
AI revenue growth depends on Gradient/GPU Droplet execution; Chief Product & Technology Officer resigned in 2025, raising execution risk on the AI inference roadmap
GPU capex intensity: keeping inventory of Nvidia H100/H200/B200 current strains a balance sheet that historically ran asset-light SMB compute

NOD.OL.company_overview: Norwegian fabless semiconductor company specializing in ultra-low-power wireless connectivity SoCs (system-on-chip). Dominant in Bluetooth Low Energy with ~40% global unit share. Sells nRF52/53/54-series BLE chips, nRF91 cellular IoT modems, and (newer) nRF7002 Wi-Fi 6 companion chips. Foundry partners are TSMC and Samsung. Revenue ~$650-700M for 2025E. Sells to ~6,000+ customers across consumer electronics, wearables, medical and industrial IoT.

revenue_mix.segment: Short-range wireless (Bluetooth LE, Thread, Matter, Wi-Fi)
Cellular IoT (LTE-M, NB-IoT, DECT NR+ via nRF91)

moat.type: BLE share leadership + nRF Connect SDK developer ecosystem
moat.narrative: Nordic's nRF Connect SDK has been the de facto reference platform for BLE developers since 2010s; engineers who learn it on a project tend to spec the same MCU on next-gen designs. >43% BLE unit share creates volume cost advantages that smaller peers like Silicon Labs and TI can't match in cents-per-chip negotiations with consumer OEMs.

key_customers: Logitech (PC peripherals)
Apple (ecosystem accessories)
Dexcom (G7 CGM uses nRF52)
SimpliSafe, Ring, smart-home OEMs
Garmin, Fitbit, wearables OEMs
key_risks: UBS Sell rating (Apr 2025) flagged 2026 growth deceleration as 2024-25 inventory restocking ends — short-range Bluetooth IC unit demand maturing
Customer concentration: top 10 customers ~40% of revenue; any wearables OEM ramp/de-spec is material
Espressif (Chinese ESP32) and Chinese BLE entrants encroaching at the low end with combo Wi-Fi+BLE parts at <50% of Nordic's ASP

MU.company_overview: Micron is one of only three global memory-chip makers, manufacturing its own DRAM (~70% of revenue) and NAND flash (~30%) as an integrated device manufacturer. It sells into data center (its biggest and fastest-growing market, driven by AI demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM), high-capacity server DIMMs and data-center SSDs), smartphones, client PCs, and embedded automotive/industrial. FY2025 (ended Aug 2025) revenue was a record $28.6 billion, up 62%, powered by the AI-driven HBM and data-center ramp; data center reached ~56% of total revenue.

revenue_mix.segment: Storage (NAND SSDs incl. data-center SSD) approx

end_markets: AI data center / cloud (HBM, server DRAM, data-center SSD)

moat.type: DRAM oligopoly + process-tech leadership + HBM design-wins qualified into Nvidia
moat.narrative: Memory is a cyclical commodity, but DRAM is a structural three-player oligopoly (Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron) protected by enormous capital intensity and leading-edge process technology (Micron's 1-gamma node). The real recent edge is HBM: Micron's HBM3E is qualified into Nvidia's Blackwell B200/GB200 platforms, and such multi-quarter qualifications plus priced, capacity-constrained supply create genuine customer lock-in. It is not a pricing-power moat in commodity DRAM, but oligopoly discipline and HBM technology leadership are meaningful advantages.

key_customers: Nvidia (HBM for Blackwell) and AMD; cloud hyperscalers (data-center DRAM/SSD); smartphone OEMs (Apple, Samsung, Android); automotive tier-1s. HBM customer base expanded to six clients
key_risks: Memory pricing cyclicality (severe boom-bust swings in DRAM/NAND)
HBM competition — SK Hynix leads and Samsung is ramping
Very high capex and fab-investment risk
China export controls and geopolitics; Chinese memory entrants (CXMT) in commodity DRAM
Inventory corrections in mobile and consumer end-markets

sources.label: Micron fiscal Q4 2025 earnings prepared remarks

AMD.company_overview: Fabless designer of x86 CPUs (EPYC server, Ryzen client), data-center GPUs (Instinct MI series), gaming GPUs (Radeon), semi-custom SoCs (PS5, Xbox), and embedded/FPGA products (post-Xilinx 2022 deal). Outsources fabrication to TSMC (5nm/3nm). FY2025 revenue $34.6B (+34%), with Data Center segment $16.6B (+32%) overtaking Client+Gaming combined as largest segment.

revenue_mix.segment: Data Center (EPYC CPUs, Instinct GPUs, Pensando DPUs)
Gaming (Radeon discrete GPUs + semi-custom PS5/Xbox SoCs)

end_markets: PC OEM (Ryzen for Dell, HP, Lenovo)
top_competitors: Broadcom (custom AI ASICs for Google, Meta)

moat.type: x86 server CPU duopoly with Intel + AI GPU optionality
moat.narrative: EPYC has taken ~30%+ x86 server CPU revenue share from Intel since 2017 via chiplet manufacturing on TSMC leading nodes — Intel's foundry struggles make this share durable through 2027. On AI, AMD is the #2 merchant GPU with $9.4B 2025 DC GPU revenue; ROCm software still trails CUDA but hyperscalers (Microsoft, Meta, Oracle) actively co-fund AMD to avoid Nvidia monopoly pricing.

key_customers: Microsoft (Azure EPYC + Instinct MI300/MI350)
Meta (MI300X for Llama inference)
Oracle, Google, AWS (EPYC server CPUs)
Sony PlayStation, Microsoft Xbox (semi-custom)
Dell, HP, Lenovo (PC OEM Ryzen)
key_risks: Nvidia CUDA software lock-in: ROCm maturity gap costs 10-30% real-world performance vs benchmarks; risk of MI400 (Helios rack) slipping vs Nvidia Rubin in 2026-27
US AI chip export controls to China: MI308 license requirements limit ~$1-2B addressable revenue; further restrictions on advanced HBM-equipped AI accelerators a recurring catalyst
Custom ASIC threat: Broadcom (Google TPU), Marvell (AWS Trainium) and Meta MTIA bypass merchant GPU buys — hyperscaler in-house silicon could cap AMD's TAM

DELL.company_overview: Dell sells servers, storage, networking, PCs, and related services to enterprises, governments, and consumers. It runs two segments: Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG) — servers (now heavily AI-optimized), storage and networking — and Client Solutions Group (CSG) — commercial and consumer PCs. AI-optimized servers are the dominant growth driver: ISG hit $19.6bn in Q4 FY2026 (+73% YoY) with AI servers up 342%, and Dell guided to ~$50bn of full-year AI-server revenue. Margins are thin (especially AI servers), so Dell earns on volume, attach (storage/services), and supply-chain scale.
end_markets: AI infrastructure / hyperscale & neocloud server build-outs

moat.type: Supply-chain scale + enterprise sales/services footprint
moat.narrative: Dell's moat is operational, not structural: a best-in-class direct-and-channel supply chain, vendor financing, global services, and entrenched enterprise relationships let it win large AI-server deals and attach proprietary PowerStore/PowerScale storage and services. There is little technology lock-in (it assembles others' GPUs/CPUs), so AI-server margins are razor-thin; the durable advantage is procurement scale, configuration/integration capability, and trusted enterprise account access.

key_customers: Hyperscalers & neoclouds (AI builders such as xAI/CoreWeave-type accounts)
Large enterprises and government agencies
Channel partners and resellers globally
key_risks: Thin and pressured AI-server gross margins; revenue mix shift toward AI servers dilutes overall profitability
Component cost inflation (memory/DRAM/HBM, GPUs) and supply allocation from Nvidia
PC demand cyclicality in CSG and dependence on a Windows refresh cycle
Customer concentration in a few large AI buyers whose capex is volatile

BESI.AS.company_overview: Dutch back-end semiconductor assembly equipment maker, specializing in die-attach tools — flip-chip bonders, thermocompression bonders (TCB) and (the strategic crown jewel) hybrid bonders used to stack chiplets at sub-micron precision for HBM, advanced logic and co-packaged optics. Sells to OSATs and IDMs. Mid-2025 raised long-term targets to €1.5-1.9B revenue at 40-55% operating margins. Applied Materials took a 9% stake in April 2025 to co-develop hybrid bonding.
end_markets: Advanced packaging for AI accelerators (HBM stacking, CoWoS)
top_competitors: ASMPT (ASM Pacific Technology) — primary die-attach rival, broader portfolio

moat.type: Hybrid-bonding placement-accuracy lead + AMAT partnership
moat.narrative: BESI hybrid bonders achieve sub-200nm placement accuracy required for advanced HBM4/3D-logic stacking — first to volume orders at TSMC and a leading logic IDM (likely Intel). 18 customers, 150+ cumulative system orders. April 2025 Applied Materials 9% strategic equity stake locks in joint roadmap for chemical/wafer-level hybrid bonding flow, foreclosing ASMPT's catch-up path.

key_customers: TSMC (CoWoS hybrid bonding for AI accelerators)
Intel (logic stacking — co-developed with Applied Materials)
OSATs: ASE, Amkor, JCET
SK Hynix, Micron, Samsung (memory packaging)
key_risks: Highly cyclical capex spending: order book swings ±50% in a quarter; hybrid-bonding ramp delays at TSMC/Intel HBM4 (now expected late-2026) could push out €100M+ of revenue
Customer concentration in 2-3 leading-edge logic/memory IDMs — any HBM4-stack architecture change (e.g., back to microbump) would re-rate the long-term €1.5-1.9B target
ASMPT and K&S TCB competition: thermocompression bonding 'good enough' for HBM3E/HBM4 base layers, limiting hybrid bonding TAM in near term

STX.company_overview: World #1 (tied with Western Digital) maker of nearline hard disk drives for cloud and enterprise storage — also legacy mission-critical, client/edge and consumer storage. FY2025 (ended June 27, 2025) revenue $9.1B (+39% YoY). Industry now a 3-vendor oligopoly: Seagate, Western Digital, Toshiba. In June 2025 launched Mozaic 3+ HAMR (heat-assisted magnetic recording) platform at 32TB+, the industry's first volume HAMR ramp.
end_markets: Hyperscale cloud (AWS, Azure, Google, Meta data lakes)
top_competitors: Solid-state alternatives: Samsung, SK Hynix, Sandisk (NAND SSDs eroding low-end HDD use cases)

moat.type: HAMR areal-density technology lead + 3-vendor HDD oligopoly
moat.narrative: HDDs are a >$25B oligopoly with effectively 2-3 producers; entry requires multi-decade R&D in head/media stacks (read/write heads, glass platters) and >$3B fab tooling. Seagate's HAMR Mozaic 3+ shipped in volume Q4 CY2024 / 1H 2025 ahead of WD's heat-assisted competitor — areal density lead translates to lower $/TB at hyperscale TCO, locking in cloud RFPs for 2026-27.

key_customers: AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Meta (hyperscaler nearline)
Backblaze, OVH, Tier-2 clouds
Dell, HPE, NetApp, Pure Storage (OEM channel)
Hikvision, Dahua (video surveillance)
key_risks: QLC NAND SSD price-per-bit declines could accelerate substitution into 'warm' storage tiers historically owned by nearline HDD — Sandisk/Solidigm 122TB QLC SSDs at $0.10/GB approaching HDD economics by 2027
HDD demand inherently tied to hyperscaler capex cycles — any 2026 AI/cloud capex digestion (CoreWeave funding hiccup, Microsoft pause) hits HDD orders with 1-2 quarter lag
HAMR yield ramp execution: Seagate's lead depends on getting HAMR volume yields up before WD's parallel ePMR/HAMR roadmap closes the gap

PRY.MI.company_overview: World's largest cable manufacturer by revenue (FY2025: €19.65B, +5.4% organic). Makes high-voltage submarine/land power cables for grid interconnectors and offshore wind, medium-voltage distribution cables, low-voltage building wire (mainly US via 2024 Encore Wire acquisition), and fiber-optic telecom cables. Operates >100 plants in 50 countries. ~40% global submarine HV cable share.

revenue_mix.segment: Transmission (HV submarine + land cables for grid interconnectors, offshore wind export)
Electrification (industrial + construction building wire, specialties — incl Encore Wire US)
Digital Solutions (fiber optic & telecom cables, datacenter cabling)

end_markets: Offshore wind farms (submarine export cables, inter-array)
Grid interconnectors (HVDC links between countries / continents)
US grid modernization & data center electrification
top_competitors: NKT (Denmark) — pure-play HV after ABB cable acquisition (~14% share)
Southwire (US building wire — direct Encore Wire competitor)

moat.type: Submarine HV cable installation vessels + €17B backlog
moat.narrative: HV submarine cable is a 3-supplier market (Prysmian, Nexans, NKT) — new entry blocked by specialized cable-lay vessels (Prysmian operates Leonardo da Vinci, Ulisse, Cable Enterprise), 3-5 year project lead times and TSO/utility pre-qualification requirements. Transmission backlog stood at €17B end-2025 (~7 years of segment revenue). Encore Wire acquisition gives US building-wire #1 share at moment of Inflation Reduction Act + data center electrification capex.

key_customers: European TSOs: TenneT, National Grid, RTE, 50Hertz, Terna (interconnectors)
Offshore wind developers: Ørsted, Iberdrola, Equinor, RWE
US utilities + electrical distributors (post-Encore Wire)
Telecom: AT&T, Verizon, Deutsche Telekom (fiber)
key_risks: Copper price volatility — Prysmian passes through but margin lag in 1-2 quarter contracts; 2025 US Section 232 copper tariff threat creates working-capital and price-mix uncertainty
Offshore wind cycle: backlog visibility strong through 2028 but inflation/permitting halted/repriced US Atlantic wind (Vineyard, Empire) — risk of cancellations / cable order push-outs

Execution risk on long-cycle HV projects: 2H 2025 disclosed margin pressure on legacy SAPEI/Tyrrhenian Link cables; one offshore install failure (cable burial, joint failure) can trigger €100M+ warranty/insurance hits

sources.label: Prysmian Q4 FY2025 press release PDF

VICR.company_overview: Vicor designs and manufactures high-density modular power components for AI servers, data centers, aerospace/defense, and industrial systems. Revenue comes from selling power modules (Bricks, Factorized Power, Vertical Power Delivery) and, increasingly, from licensing its IP portfolio to OEMs and hyperscalers building proprietary power architectures. Vertical integration via its Andover, Massachusetts ChiP fab is core to the model.

revenue_mix.segment: Advanced Products (NBM, VPD, Factorized Power, royalties)

moat.type: Patent portfolio + vertical fab integration
moat.narrative: Vicor owns foundational IP on Factorized Power Architecture, NBM, and Vertical Power Delivery for sub-1V high-current AI accelerator rails; it has won multiple ITC injunctions in 2025 against Chinese copy-cat suppliers, forcing OEMs and hyperscalers to take licenses. Royalty revenue now exceeds R&D spend and is targeted to double over 2 years.

key_customers: Hyperscale cloud providers (unnamed, concentrated)
Leading AI accelerator OEMs (likely NVIDIA ecosystem ODMs)
Defense primes via aerospace channel
key_risks: Heavy customer concentration in a handful of hyperscalers and one AI accelerator design platform — order timing is lumpy
China revenue ~12% exposed to export controls and to Chinese domestic SiC/power-module substitution
Royalty income depends on continued IP enforcement victories; an adverse ITC or appellate ruling would crater the licensing thesis

sources.label: BeyondSPX - Vicor IP and VPD analysis

FLEX.company_overview: Flex is a global #2-3 Electronics Manufacturing Services (EMS) provider with FY25 revenue of ~$25.8B. It designs, manufactures, assembles, and supplies finished products and embedded systems for OEMs across data center, automotive, industrial, healthcare, and consumer markets. Revenue is from contract manufacturing fees plus growing value-added services (design, supply chain orchestration, embedded power).

revenue_mix.segment: Flex Agility Solutions (FAS) - cloud, consumer, lifestyle, mobile
Flex Reliability Solutions (FRS) - auto, industrial, health, capital equip, power

end_markets: AI data center / cloud infrastructure (CDS sub-segment)

moat.type: Scale + high-mix manufacturing footprint + sticky design-in relationships
moat.narrative: Flex differentiates from Foxconn-scale players by owning embedded power (Anord Mardix data-center power-pod franchise) and high-mix Reliability Solutions where switching costs are high once a product is qualified into FDA-regulated, automotive, or hyperscaler programs. Reliability segment generates 5%+ operating margin vs. EMS industry 3-4%.

key_customers: Hyperscaler data-center customers (CDS power pods)
Major automotive OEMs (compute and power electronics)
Medical device leaders (Health Solutions)
key_risks: FAS exposure to consumer device demand softness — cloud/AI ramp must offset lifestyle decline
Tariff and reshoring policy whiplash (Mexico, China) raises capex and working capital needs
Margin compression risk in commoditized assembly as Foxconn pushes into US data-center build-out (e.g. NVIDIA Houston)

COHR.company_overview: Coherent is a vertically integrated optics and compound-semiconductor supplier. It makes 800G/1.6T optical transceivers, lasers, and engineered materials (silicon carbide, indium phosphide) sold to AI data center hyperscalers, telecom carriers, semiconductor equipment makers, and industrial laser end users. FY25 revenue was $5.81B (+23% YoY), driven primarily by AI datacom transceivers.
end_markets: Industrial cutting/welding lasers and display annealing

moat.type: Vertical integration in InP and SiC + scarce optical capacity
moat.narrative: Coherent owns end-to-end InP epi/wafer/laser/transceiver capability — one of few suppliers (with Lumentum) that NVIDIA picked for its $4B March 2026 priority-capacity investment to back 800G/1.6T and CPO. Six-inch InP wafer capability and Sherman, TX fab create a multi-year lead on Chinese rivals.

key_customers: NVIDIA (CPO partner + capacity reservation)
Cisco/Arista (datacom transceivers)
ASML, Applied Materials (laser annealing)
Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Meta, Google) via switch OEMs
key_risks: Datacom transceiver concentration — book-to-bill >4x is great but creates whiplash if hyperscaler capex pauses in 2026-27
Materials/SiC segment in decline due to weak auto EV demand and Wolfspeed/Chinese price war
Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) could displace pluggable revenue late-decade if hyperscalers move to switch-integrated optics

WDC.company_overview: Post-SanDisk spinoff (Feb 2025), Western Digital is a pure-play hard disk drive maker. ~100% of revenue comes from HDDs, dominated by high-capacity nearline drives sold into cloud and AI data centers. Manufactures in Thailand and Malaysia with R&D centered in Fremont/Irvine.
end_markets: Hyperscale cloud storage (AI training data lakes, exabyte-scale)
top_competitors: Seagate Technology (STX) - duopoly partner in HDD

moat.type: HDD duopoly + areal-density tech leadership
moat.narrative: HDD is a structural duopoly with Seagate (~63/37 share favoring WDC by Q1 2025); 30+ years of accumulated head/media IP and capital intensity mean no new entrant is plausible. ePMR and incoming HAMR/UltraSMR technology lets WDC ship 32TB+ nearline drives where SSDs are still ~6x the $/TB cost for cold/warm data.

key_customers: Top-10 customers = 73% of revenue
3 customers each >10% (one ~18%, ~16%, ~13%) — almost certainly Microsoft, Meta, AWS/Google class hyperscalers
Major OEMs (Dell, HPE, Lenovo)
key_risks: Top-3 customer concentration ~47% — order pauses by any one hyperscaler can swing a quarter
QLC NAND price erosion could pull-in HDD/SSD crossover for nearline 2-3 years earlier than expected
Cyclical glut risk after current AI capex super-cycle — historical HDD industry has seen 30%+ revenue drops

TTMI.company_overview: TTM Technologies is North America's largest printed circuit board (PCB) and RF components manufacturer, with FY25 revenue ~$2.9B. It sells highly engineered PCBs and RF subassemblies primarily to US aerospace & defense primes plus commercial AI/data-center and networking customers. ~18,200 employees across 24 facilities in North America and Asia.
end_markets: US defense radar/EW programs (F-35, Patriot, Aegis)
top_competitors: Founder Tech, Gold Circuit (Asian commercial PCB)

moat.type: Trusted/cleared US-based defense PCB supply + record backlog
moat.narrative: TTM is one of very few US-domiciled, security-cleared 'Trusted Supplier' PCB fabs for DoD programs — most rivals offshored decades ago. Defense backlog hit a record $1.61B in 2025 giving multi-year visibility; new Syracuse defense PCB facility (DoD-funded $42M) deepens the moat.

key_customers: Raytheon Technologies / RTX (Integrated Defense Systems)
Lockheed Martin
John Deere
Hyperscaler AI server ODMs (Penang facility ramping)
key_risks: Heavy A&D concentration tied to US defense budget appropriations and program timing
China commercial PCB segment squeezed by domestic Chinese substrate makers — TTM has announced China site review/exits
AI commercial ramp at new Penang fab carries execution risk; yields and qualification with hyperscalers must hit ramp curve

CIEN.company_overview: Ciena builds the optical and routing systems that move data across long-haul, metro and data-center-interconnect networks - the physical 'backbone' that carries internet and AI traffic between facilities. Revenue comes mostly from selling coherent optical transport hardware (WaveLogic-powered platforms), plus a higher-margin layer of network-automation software (Blue Planet, MCP) and global installation/maintenance services. Once a telco or hyperscaler standardizes on Ciena's gear, they keep buying capacity upgrades from it for years.

moat.type: Coherent optical DSP leadership (WaveLogic) + entrenched carrier installed base
moat.narrative: Ciena's vertically-integrated WaveLogic coherent DSP/optics keeps it at or near the technology frontier on bits-per-wavelength and power-per-bit, the metric hyperscalers optimize for; combined with ~51% North American optical share it forces rivals to out-engineer a moving target. Multi-year carrier and webscale capacity contracts plus embedded MCP/Blue Planet management software raise switching costs, since ripping out the transport layer mid-lifecycle is operationally painful.

key_customers: AT&T (long-standing Tier-1, ~top-3 customer)
Hyperscalers - Amazon/AWS, Google, Meta, Microsoft (now >54% of revenue)
Verizon
Large global telcos & subsea consortia
key_risks: Severe customer concentration - top 3 customers ~44% of Q4 revenue; one hyperscaler alone ~18%; any capex pause hits hard
Dependence on the hyperscaler AI/cloud capex cycle, which could decelerate sharply if AI build-out moderates
Nokia-Infinera combination intensifies optical competition and pricing pressure
Merchant silicon (Broadcom, Marvell) commoditizing parts of the optical stack and pulling some DCI in-house at hyperscalers
Lumpy, order-driven revenue with long sales cycles; gross-margin mix shifts as low-margin webscale hardware grows

sources.label: Ciena FY2025 Q4 earnings press release (8-K)
SDxCentral - Ciena AI wave & customer concentration

SUBC.OL.company_overview: Subsea 7 is one of the world's two largest subsea EPCI (Engineering, Procurement, Construction, Installation) contractors. It designs, builds and installs deepwater oil & gas production systems (SURF, conventional, life-of-field) and offshore wind foundations/inter-array cables, operating a global fleet of ~40 specialized vessels. FY25 revenue $7.1B, Adj. EBITDA $1.5B (+36% YoY).
end_markets: Deepwater oil & gas (Brazil pre-salt, Guyana, Norway, Angola)
Offshore wind farm foundations (Dogger Bank, East Anglia, Taiwan)
top_competitors: Aker Solutions, Heerema Marine Contractors (specialized HLV)

moat.type: Scarce specialized vessel fleet + integrated EPCI track record
moat.narrative: Subsea pipelay/heavy-lift vessels (Seven Borealis, Seven Vega) take 4-5 years and $500M+ to build; the global fleet is owned by 4-5 firms. 25+ years of supermajor delivery history with Equinor, Shell, TotalEnergies, BP creates qualified-vendor lock-in. Pending Saipem merger (Saipem7, expected H2 2026) would create €43B backlog colossus.

key_customers: Equinor (Fram Sør FEED Jan 2025, multiple awards)
Petrobras (Brazil pre-salt)
Shell, BP, TotalEnergies, ExxonMobil, Eni, Chevron
SSE/Equinor (Dogger Bank), ScottishPower (East Anglia THREE)
key_risks: EC antitrust review of Saipem merger — major oil supermajors have lobbied against approval citing consolidation harm
Renewables segment margin (16.6%) materially lower than O&G (22.6%); mix shift could compress group EBITDA margin if wind grows faster than oil

ON.company_overview: onsemi (ON) is a focused power and sensing semiconductor company. The remaining structural advantages are the enormous x86 server/PC installed base and software compatibility, and being the only US-headquartered company attempting leading-edge logic (18A), which carries strategic/government backing. The thesis hinges on 18A yields and landing external foundry customers; today the moat is more policy and legacy than technology leadership.

key_customers: Dell, HP, Lenovo, Asus (PC OEMs)
Hyperscalers (AWS, Microsoft, Google for server CPUs)
Foundry: external customers being courted (e.g. Microsoft, US government work)
key_risks: Intel 18A yield/ramp execution risk — the entire turnaround depends on it
Continued CPU share loss to AMD and Arm-based server/PC chips
Absence of a competitive AI accelerator vs Nvidia in the largest data-center growth pool
Heavy capex/foundry losses straining the balance sheet; China exposure (~28%) and export-control risk; dilution from US government equity stake

TEM.L.company: Templeton Emerging Markets Investment Trust plc
TEM.L.company_overview: TEM is a London-listed closed-end investment trust (not an operating company) that invests in listed equities of emerging-market companies, managed by Franklin Templeton. It makes money for shareholders via NAV growth and dividends from a diversified EM equity portfolio; the manager earns a management fee on net assets. Launched 1989, it is one of the longest-running dedicated EM trusts. Its 'revenue mix' below is portfolio sector allocation rather than business segments, and it typically trades at a discount to NAV.
end_markets: Retail and institutional UK investors seeking EM exposure

moat.type: Franklin Templeton EM research franchise + closed-end structure (no structural moat)
moat.narrative: As an investment trust this has no business moat — it competes on manager skill, fees, and discount/premium dynamics. Its edge, if any, is Franklin Templeton's long-tenured EM research team and on-the-ground analyst network, plus the closed-end structure that lets the manager hold less-liquid positions without forced redemptions. It is structurally challenged by cheap passive EM ETFs; the trust must justify active fees through alpha and discount-narrowing buybacks.

key_customers: UK retail and wealth-management investors
Discretionary fund managers / multi-asset allocators
Self-directed ISA/SIPP holders on UK platforms
key_risks: Persistent discount to NAV eroding shareholder returns regardless of portfolio performance
Heavy Greater-China weighting (~45%) exposes it to China policy, property and geopolitical risk
Active management underperforming cheap EM index ETFs (fee pressure / passive competition)
Currency risk (EM FX vs GBP) and EM equity-market volatility

OGN.company_overview: Organon is a global pharmaceutical company spun off from Merck in 2021, focused on women's health, biosimilars, and a large portfolio of 'established brands' (off-patent legacy medicines). It markets 70+ products across ~140 markets. Revenue comes from three franchises: Women's Health (contraceptives like Nexplanon, fertility), Biosimilars (e.g. Hadlima/adalimumab), and Established Brands (legacy cardiovascular, respiratory, etc., several past patent loss). It carries significant debt from the spin-off and is managing the trade-off between dividend, deleveraging, and reinvestment.

geo_mix.region: Asia Pacific / Japan / LatAm / rest of world

end_markets: Retail and hospital pharmacy across emerging + developed markets

moat.type: Established global distribution + Nexplanon franchise; weak structural moat
moat.narrative: Organon's durable asset is Nexplanon, a long-acting reversible contraceptive with device/implant complexity and physician familiarity that creates a real but time-limited barrier (a generic threat looms as patents wind down). Its broader moat is a wide international distribution and regulatory footprint across 140 markets that biosimilars can ride. Otherwise the established-brands portfolio is structurally declining off patent cliffs; the company competes on scale and channel, not innovation, making it more a cash-harvest/biosimilar-pivot story than a wide-moat franchise.

key_customers: Wholesalers/distributors (McKesson, Cencora, Cardinal in US)
National health systems and tenders (ex-US)
Hospital and retail pharmacy channels
Family-planning / public-health programs (contraceptives)
key_risks: Nexplanon generic/LOE risk — its single most important growth driver faces eventual competition
Established Brands in structural decline (Atozet, Singulair losses of exclusivity, esp. China/Japan/Europe)
High leverage from the Merck spin-off constrains flexibility; dividend was cut to prioritize deleveraging
China volume-based procurement (VBP) pricing pressure and US drug-pricing/IRA policy risk

AFRM.company_overview: Affirm is a US buy-now-pay-later (BNPL) lender. It lets shoppers split purchases into installments at checkout — both interest-bearing and 0% APR (merchant-subsidized) loans — and integrates with merchants and platforms. It earns money via merchant fees, consumer interest income, interchange on its Affirm Card, and gains on selling loans to capital partners. FY2025 GMV was ~$36bn (+35% YoY) across ~358,000 active merchants. Its capital-light model relies on funding partners and securitization to fund originations rather than holding all loans on balance sheet.

revenue_mix.segment: Gain on sales of loans (to capital partners)

end_markets: Marketplaces / platforms (Shopify Shop Pay Installments, Amazon)
Everyday spend via the Affirm Card

moat.type: Underwriting data + enterprise platform integrations; contestable network effect
moat.narrative: Affirm's edge is item-level transaction underwriting (no late fees, priced per transaction) built on years of repayment data, plus deep platform integrations — it is the exclusive US Shop Pay Installments provider for Shopify and is integrated with Amazon — giving distribution that's hard for newcomers to replicate quickly. The moat is real but contestable: it lost Walmart exclusivity to Klarna, top-5 partners are ~46% of GMV, and BNPL has low switching costs for consumers, so the advantage rests on credit performance and merchant relationships rather than a structural lock.

key_customers: Shopify (exclusive US Shop Pay Installments partner)
Amazon (integrated checkout)
Top 5 merchants/platforms ~46% of GMV (concentration)
Travel (airlines/OTAs) and electronics retailers
key_risks: Credit/funding risk: rising delinquencies or capital-market stress raises funding cost and loan-sale gains volatility
Loss of key partners (lost Walmart to Klarna) and high top-5 GMV concentration (~46%)
Regulatory: CFPB BNPL rules, potential interest-rate/disclosure requirements
Interest-rate sensitivity (funding cost) and competition from Klarna, PayPal and card issuers compressing economics

IRDM.company_overview: Iridium owns and operates the only commercial satellite constellation (66 cross-linked LEO satellites) providing voice and data coverage over 100% of the Earth, including poles and oceans where terrestrial and geostationary networks cannot reach. It makes money mainly from recurring airtime/subscription service revenue sold wholesale through ~500 partners and a fixed long-term U.S. government EMSS contract, plus device/equipment sales and engineering work.
end_markets: Land mobile & personal (emergency SOS, satellite phones)

moat.type: Unique global LEO constellation + regulatory spectrum + DoD lock-in
moat.narrative: Iridium is the only network with truly pole-to-pole, cross-linked LEO coverage and holds globally harmonized L-band spectrum that is hard to replicate; the sole-source U.S. government EMSS contract (~$257M in 2025) and the engineered-in nature of its IoT/safety modules create high switching costs. The constellation is fully deployed and paid for, so incremental subscribers carry very high margins.

key_customers: U.S. Department of Defense (EMSS, ~29% of total revenue)
Garmin (inReach / SOS modules)
Caterpillar, John Deere (asset telematics)
Qualcomm (Snapdragon Satellite, since wound down)
key_risks: Direct-to-cell competition from SpaceX Starlink and Apple/Globalstar eroding the high-margin niche over the next decade
Single-constellation concentration — a launch or in-orbit failure of the aging fleet (deployed 2017-2019) would be catastrophic; next-gen replacement capex looms
U.S. government revenue concentration (~29%) tied to one contract subject to budget/political risk

PCT.L.company_overview: Polar Capital Technology Trust is a London-listed closed-end investment trust (not an operating company) that invests in a global portfolio of technology equities, aiming for long-term capital growth. It has no operating revenue in the conventional sense; shareholder returns come from NAV growth and the management team's stock selection. Investors are effectively buying a diversified, actively managed basket of global tech names, often at a discount to NAV.
top_competitors: Direct tech ETFs (e.g. iShares S&P 500 IT, Nasdaq-100 trackers)

moat.type: Active management track record + investment-trust structure
moat.narrative: No structural moat — this is a fund. Its only edge is the Polar Capital technology team's long-run stock-picking record and the closed-end structure (permanent capital, no forced redemptions, ability to use gearing). Differentiation vs a cheap passive tracker rests entirely on whether active selection plus a discount-to-NAV entry can beat the index after fees — historically inconsistent.

key_customers: NVIDIA (~7.5% of portfolio)
Meta Platforms (~7.3%)
Microsoft (~6.8%)
Apple, Alphabet, TSMC (top-15 positions)
key_risks: Concentration in mega-cap AI/semiconductor names (top 15 ~57% of long positions) — a tech/AI drawdown hits NAV hard
Persistent discount to NAV can widen, compounding share-price losses beyond the underlying portfolio
Fee drag and active-vs-passive risk: must outperform low-cost Nasdaq/IT trackers to justify the wrapper

sources.label: Polar Capital Technology Trust top holdings update

SYNA.company_overview: Synaptics designs mixed-signal and embedded semiconductors plus software for human-machine interface and connectivity. It started in touchpads/fingerprint sensors for laptops and phones and has pivoted toward Edge AI, IoT connectivity (Wi-Fi/Bluetooth/Thread combos), and wireless processors. Revenue comes from selling chips into PC OEMs, consumer/IoT device makers, automotive infotainment, and enterprise/networking equipment.

revenue_mix.segment: Enterprise & Automotive (docking, video interface, auto displays)
Core IoT (Wi-Fi/BT connectivity, Edge AI processors)

moat.type: Embedded design wins + IP in low-power Edge AI/connectivity
moat.narrative: Switching costs come from being designed into customer hardware reference designs with long product cycles, plus a large patent portfolio in touch/connectivity. The newer Astra Edge AI and Veros/SiW connectivity lines aim to combine low-power Wi-Fi with on-device AI — a genuinely differentiated niche — but the legacy mobile/PC franchises are commoditizing and the moat is narrowing to specific design-win pockets, not structural.

key_customers: Major PC OEMs (Dell, HP, Lenovo via docking/display)
Consumer/IoT device makers
Google (Edge AI / connectivity partnerships)
Automotive Tier-1 display suppliers
key_risks: Heavy China exposure (~38% ship-to) amid U.S.-China semiconductor trade/export-control risk
Structural decline of legacy Mobile segment (~20%, falling) and PC cyclicality
Execution risk on the Core IoT/Edge AI pivot — must scale design wins fast enough to offset legacy erosion against well-capitalized rivals (Qualcomm, Infineon)

GFS.company_overview: GlobalFoundries is a pure-play semiconductor contract manufacturer (foundry) — it makes chips designed by others. Unlike TSMC, it deliberately does not chase the leading-edge race; instead it specializes in differentiated, feature-rich process technologies (RF-SOI, FinFET, FDX/22FDX, silicon photonics, power, BCD) for mature and specialty nodes. Revenue comes from wafer fabrication contracts with ~250+ customers, many under long-term agreements with capacity reservations and prepayments.

moat.type: Differentiated specialty processes + sticky design wins + reshoring/trusted-foundry status
moat.narrative: GF's moat is owning leadership in specialty nodes (e.g. RF-SOI for nearly every premium smartphone's RF front-end, 22FDX for ultra-low-power IoT, photonics) where re-qualifying a chip at another foundry costs years and millions, so design wins are extremely sticky. Its U.S./EU/Singapore fab footprint makes it a 'trusted', geopolitically de-risked source for U.S. DoD and automotive customers wanting supply outside Taiwan — a structural tailwind from reshoring and the CHIPS Act.

key_customers: Qualcomm (RF front-end, largest customer, long-term agreement)
AMD (legacy WSA wafer supply agreement)
Apple supply chain (RF/connectivity)
NXP, Infineon, Bosch (automotive)
U.S. Department of Defense (trusted foundry)
key_risks: Smartphone cyclicality and concentration (Smart Mobile ~41%, Qualcomm largest customer ~ top-10 are 63% of wafers)
Trailing-edge price pressure and aggressive capacity additions from Chinese foundries (SMIC, Hua Hong)
Capital intensity and underutilization risk — fabs are fixed-cost heavy, so demand troughs crush margins

RKLB.company_overview: Rocket Lab is a vertically integrated space company. It earns revenue two ways: (1) Launch Services — flying small satellites to orbit on its Electron rocket (and the suborbital HASTE variant), with the larger medium-lift Neutron rocket in development; and (2) Space Systems — building and selling satellites, spacecraft components (reaction wheels, solar arrays, star trackers, separation systems, radios) and operating satellites/constellations for customers. Space Systems is now the larger, faster-growing part.
end_markets: U.S. government & defense (Space Force, SDA, NRO, DARPA)
top_competitors: Northrop Grumman, L3Harris, Airbus, Terran Orbital (space systems/components)

moat.type: Only proven small-launch operator + vertical integration into a components flywheel
moat.narrative: Rocket Lab is the only Western company with a reliably operational dedicated small-launch vehicle (Electron, 21 missions in 2025 at 100% success), giving it a near-monopoly on responsive dedicated small launch while rivals struggle to reach orbit. Its vertical integration — owning the component lines (via acquisitions like Sinclair, SolAero, Planetary Systems) used inside its own and rivals' satellites — creates a flywheel and switching costs; the in-development Neutron aims to break into the much larger medium-lift/constellation deployment market against SpaceX.

key_customers: U.S. Space Force / Space Development Agency
NRO and other U.S. national-security agencies
NASA (civil missions)
Commercial constellation operators (e.g. Synspective, BlackSky, Kineis)
key_risks: Neutron execution risk — schedule slips and cost overruns on the unproven medium-lift rocket that the growth thesis depends on
Not yet consistently profitable; heavy R&D/capex burn and reliance on capital markets
SpaceX's dominance and aggressive pricing (Transporter rideshare) caps Electron pricing power and Neutron's addressable share

sources.label: Rocket Lab Q4 & FY2025 results press release

CORT.company_overview: Corcept sells prescription drugs that block the cortisol (glucocorticoid) receptor. Its cash engine is Korlym (mifepristone 300mg) plus its own authorized generic, prescribed in the U.S. for endogenous Cushing's syndrome/hypercortisolism and dispensed through a controlled specialty-pharmacy network. In March 2026 the FDA approved Lifyorli (relacorilant) with nab-paclitaxel for platinum-resistant ovarian cancer, giving Corcept a second, oncology revenue stream. Every asset in the pipeline is a variation on the same idea: selectively antagonise cortisol signalling. 2026 revenue guidance was raised to $1.1-$1.2bn.

revenue_mix.segment: Lifyorli (relacorilant) — platinum-resistant ovarian cancer, launched Mar-2026

geo_mix.region: United States (both products are U.S.-only today)
Europe (MAA for relacorilant in PROC under EMA review; approval guided by YE-2026)

end_markets: Endocrinology — endogenous Cushing's syndrome and the much larger undiagnosed hypercortisolism pool (CATALYST/MOMENTUM screening data in difficult-to-control diabetes and hypertension)
Gynecologic oncology — platinum-resistant ovarian cancer (Lifyorli + nab-paclitaxel is an NCCN preferred regimen since Apr-2026)
Solid-tumour oncology pipeline — endometrial, cervical, pancreatic, prostate (BELLA/STELLA/TRIDENT/SYNERGY)
Hepatology — MASH (miricorilant, Phase 2b MONARCH reads out YE-2026)
top_competitors: Recordati (Isturisa/osilodrostat, Signifor) — the main branded rival in Cushing's
Teva and other ANDA filers on mifepristone 300mg — Corcept pre-empted with its own authorized generic
AbbVie (Elahere/mirvetuximab) — the incumbent in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer, but requires FRalpha biomarker selection, which Lifyorli does not
Surgery/pituitary-directed therapy and generic ketoconazole as off-label alternatives in Cushing's

moat.type: Category creation plus a controlled distribution and diagnosis funnel
moat.narrative: Corcept spent a decade building the only U.S. commercial infrastructure aimed at finding hypercortisolic patients — specialty pharmacy, cortisol testing support, and an endocrinology sales force — so it captures demand it itself creates rather than competing for existing scripts. Relacorilant/Lifyorli extends that by being a selective GR antagonist without mifepristone's progesterone-receptor liability, and in ovarian cancer it is the rare targeted agent that needs no biomarker test, which lowers the friction of adding it to nab-paclitaxel. The fragility is that the entire franchise rests on one mechanism and one molecule class; there is no platform diversification to fall back on.

key_customers: U.S. specialty pharmacy network (Corcept transitioned to a new pharmacy vendor in Feb-2026; Korlym is not sold at retail)
Academic and community endocrinology practices treating Cushing's syndrome
Gynecologic-oncology practices — over 1,300 patients started Lifyorli in its first full quarter
Commercial payers and Medicare Part D — no single named end customer is disclosed
key_risks: Korlym + authorized generic is still ~81% of revenue and faces generic mifepristone entry; any share loss hits the profit base directly
Relacorilant for Cushing's already drew a Complete Response Letter once; the resubmitted NDA has a PDUFA date of 17-Dec-2026 and a second CRL would strand the largest label expansion
Launch spend is compressing margins — Q2-26 SG&A was $156.9m vs $103.9m a year earlier, and H1-26 GAAP operating result was a $8.3m loss despite 20% revenue growth
Single-mechanism concentration: Korlym, Lifyorli, nenocorilant, miricorilant and dazucorilant are all cortisol modulators, so a class-level safety finding would hit everything at once
Lifyorli's PROC opportunity is a narrow, heavily-contested niche where AbbVie's Elahere is entrenched in FRalpha-positive patients

sources.label: Q2 2026 results and corporate update (8-K Ex-99.1, 29-Jul-2026)

ATT.L.company_overview: Allianz Technology Trust is a London-listed closed-end investment trust (not an operating company) that invests in a concentrated global portfolio of technology equities, run by AllianzGI's San Francisco-based technology team. It generates no operating revenue; shareholder returns come from NAV growth driven by stock selection, plus any narrowing of the share-price discount to NAV. Investors are buying an actively managed, US-tech-heavy basket aiming to find the 'next Apple, Google or Microsoft.'
top_competitors: Passive tech ETFs (Nasdaq-100 / S&P 500 IT trackers)

moat.type: Active management track record + closed-end structure
moat.narrative: No structural moat — it is a fund. Its edge is the AllianzGI San Francisco team's high-conviction, benchmark-beating stock-picking record (it outperformed its index in 2025) and the closed-end structure's permanent capital and gearing. The investment case rests entirely on active selection plus a discount entry beating low-cost passive tech trackers after fees, with very high concentration in mega-cap AI/semis.

key_customers: NVIDIA (~10.3% of portfolio, top holding)
Alphabet (~9.4%)
Microsoft (~8.0%)
Apple (~7.2%), Broadcom (~7.2%), TSMC, Micron, Lam Research, Meta, KLA (top 10)
key_risks: Extreme concentration — ~92% US, top holdings dominated by AI/semiconductor mega-caps; an AI/tech drawdown hits NAV severely
Discount-to-NAV volatility can amplify share-price losses beyond the portfolio
Active-vs-passive risk and fee drag: must consistently beat cheap Nasdaq/IT trackers to justify the wrapper

CCC.L.company_overview: Computacenter is a European IT reseller and services provider. The bulk of its money flows through Technology Sourcing — procuring and reselling hardware, software and cloud licences from vendors (HPE, Cisco, Microsoft, Dell, NVIDIA, etc.) to large corporate and public-sector clients, a high-volume, thin-margin distribution business. The higher-margin, stickier part is Services — managing, integrating and supporting customers' IT estates (data centre, networking, workplace, professional and managed services).

moat.type: Scale procurement + vendor relationships + embedded managed-services stickiness
moat.narrative: The reseller business is structurally low-margin and not deeply moated, but Computacenter's scale earns it top-tier rebate/partner status with vendors (HPE, Cisco, Microsoft, NVIDIA) and access to constrained AI/data-centre supply that smaller resellers can't get. The real stickiness is in long-term managed-services and workplace contracts embedded in clients' operations, where it holds the customer relationship and switching is painful — the North America hyperscale ramp is the current growth engine.

key_customers: Large UK/European enterprises and FTSE/DAX corporates
UK and German government/public sector
US enterprise and hyperscale (cloud) customers driving North America growth
Financial-services and industrial blue-chips
key_risks: Wafer-thin gross margins on Technology Sourcing (~82% of revenue) — small volume or rebate shifts swing profit; revenue is partly low-quality pass-through GII
Customer/segment concentration in hyperscale networking & data-centre spend that can be lumpy and cyclical
German public-sector softness and FX translation (large euro/dollar revenue vs sterling reporting); AI-driven hardware demand could normalize quickly

QCOM.company_overview: Qualcomm makes money two ways: (1) QCT, its chip business, designs Snapdragon system-on-chips and modems that power most premium Android phones and increasingly cars, PCs and IoT devices; and (2) QTL, a high-margin licensing business that collects royalties on essentially every 3G/4G/5G handset sold worldwide because Qualcomm owns foundational cellular-standard patents. QTL is small in revenue but throws off outsized profit; QCT is the volume engine now diversifying away from smartphones into automotive and IoT.

revenue_mix.segment: QCT - IoT (PC, XR, industrial, edge AI)

end_markets: IoT, XR/AR headsets, industrial edge AI

moat.type: Foundational cellular SEP patent portfolio + integrated modem-to-antenna RF leadership
moat.narrative: QTL's standard-essential 3G/4G/5G patents force virtually every handset maker to pay Qualcomm a royalty regardless of whose chip is inside - a near-tollbooth on the entire industry that funds R&D. In chips, Qualcomm's lead in integrated premium modems and the full RF front-end (modem-to-antenna) plus Snapdragon's flagship Android dominance gives pricing power; Apple's own modem-study rebuttal and analysts' 5G-Advanced R&D-edge view underscore the technology gap rivals must close.

key_customers: Samsung (largest single SoC customer, deepening partnership)
Xiaomi, Oppo, Vivo, Honor and other Chinese OEMs
Apple (modems only, declining - ~20% of iPhones by 2026, zero by 2027)
Auto OEMs (BMW, Mercedes, GM and others via Digital Chassis)
key_risks: Apple in-housing modems (C-series) eliminates a major QCT customer - none of iPhone by FY2027
Extreme China concentration (~46% of revenue) exposes Qualcomm to US-China trade/export and demand cyclicality
QTL royalty stream pressured by license expirations - Huawei royalties already dropped out in FY25; renewal timing drives lumpiness
MediaTek share gains in mid-range and pushing into premium Android; Samsung in-house Exynos competition
Smartphone is a mature, ~flat market - growth thesis hinges on auto + IoT + PC ramps hitting 2029 targets

BMPS.MI.company: Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena S.p.A.
BMPS.MI.company_overview: Monte dei Paschi di Siena is Italy's oldest bank and now its third-largest banking group following the September-2025 acquisition of 86.3% of investment bank Mediobanca. The core business is traditional retail and commercial banking - taking deposits and lending to ~3.4 million Italian households and SMEs, concentrated in Tuscany and central Italy - earning net interest income plus fees from wealth management, payments and bancassurance. The Mediobanca deal bolts on investment banking, consumer finance and private banking, transforming MPS from a turnaround retail bank into a diversified national champion.

revenue_mix.segment: Net fees & commissions (wealth mgmt, payments, bancassurance)

end_markets: Wealth management & private banking (incl. online bank Widiba)
top_competitors: Intesa Sanpaolo (largest Italian bank; launched a counter-bid for MPS in June 2026)

moat.type: Entrenched regional deposit franchise + restored capital strength + DTA tax shield
moat.narrative: MPS's ~1,300-branch network with deep roots in Tuscany (287 branches, ~22% local share) gives a sticky low-cost retail deposit base that is expensive for rivals to replicate. Years of restructuring left it with a large stock of deferred tax assets (the Mediobanca merger alone is projected to unlock ~EUR500m of DTA accretion over six years) that shields future profits, and a cost-income ratio improved to ~45% makes it a structurally cheaper operator post-turnaround.

key_customers: ~3.4 million Italian retail customers (mass-market & affluent)
Italian SMEs and mid-corporates
Widiba online-bank clients (~0.3m managed exclusively)
Private-banking & wealth clients (expanded via Mediobanca/Banca Generali)
key_risks: Live takeover battle - Intesa Sanpaolo launched a ~EUR30.6B unsolicited bid for MPS in June 2026, creating strategic and ownership uncertainty
Mediobanca integration complexity (86.3% stake, merger by incorporation, minority squeeze-out) plus Generali/Banca Generali entanglements
Italian sovereign / rate sensitivity - heavy domestic BTP holdings and NII exposure to ECB rate cuts
Italian Treasury still a large legacy shareholder (was 26.7%, mandated to fall below 20%) - political overhang on strategy

MB.MI.company: Mediobanca - Banca di Credito Finanziario S.p.A.
MB.MI.company_overview: Mediobanca is Italy's leading investment bank, now operating as a diversified financial group across four engines: Wealth Management (private banking, asset management, premier clients), Consumer Finance (Compass - personal loans, BNPL via Pagolight), Corporate & Investment Banking (M&A advisory, lending, capital markets - increasingly cross-border), and Insurance/Principal Investing centered on a ~13% strategic stake in insurer Assicurazioni Generali. end_markets: Large corporates & PE (M&A advisory, lending, ECM/DCM)
Insurance income via Generali equity stake

moat.narrative: Mediobanca owns the deepest blue-chip advisory relationships in Italy - the go-to adviser on domestic M&A and capital markets - a reputational franchise built over decades that newcomers cannot replicate. Compass's consumer-finance book runs at a ~9.6% ROA, an unusually profitable scaled BNPL/personal-loan platform, while the ~13% Generali stake provides a stable, bank-cycle-decoupled earnings stream and strategic optionality (it underpinned both the Banca Generali bid and resistance to the MPS takeover).

HNW / affluent private-banking clients
Mass-market consumer borrowers (Compass)

Assicurazioni Generali (associate / strategic holding)

Generali stake entanglement and the contested Banca Generali exchange offer; governance/share-swap disputes under investigation
CIB advisory & trading revenues are cyclical and tied to volatile deal/market activity
Consumer Finance (Compass) credit-cost sensitivity if Italian unemployment or rates rise
Concentration in the mature, low-growth Italian economy; ECB rate cuts compress net interest income

PANW.company_overview: Palo Alto Networks is the largest pure-play cybersecurity vendor, selling protection across three platforms: Strata (network security - next-gen firewalls, hardware and software/SASE), Prisma (cloud security - securing cloud-native apps and remote access), and Cortex (AI-driven security operations, including the XSIAM SOC platform). Revenue is increasingly subscription and support (~80% of total) rather than appliance hardware, and the company is pushing 'platformization' - getting customers to consolidate multiple security tools onto its integrated stack, tracked via Next-Generation Security ARR.

moat.type: Platform consolidation + high switching costs + AI-led SOC data gravity
moat.narrative: Palo Alto's 'platformization' strategy (~1,250+ platformizations) locks customers into a multi-product security suite, so ripping out one module means re-architecting their whole defense - driving 32% NGS ARR growth to $5.6B and strong net retention. Cortex XSIAM's AI-driven SOC accumulates telemetry data gravity that improves detection the more it ingests, and consolidating fragmented point tools onto one vendor is a structural tailwind PANW is best-positioned to capture given the breadth of its Strata/Prisma/Cortex footprint.

Government & defense agencies
Financial-services and healthcare security teams
Managed security service providers (MSSPs/MDR partners)

Legacy firewall/product hardware revenue declining as the mix shifts to software/SaaS - the transition must keep pace
Aggressive M&A-driven expansion raises integration and execution risk across an ever-broader portfolio
Rich valuation leaves little room for ARR/billings disappointment; demand sensitive to enterprise security-budget cycles
Customer concentration on large deals and 'free product' platformization incentives can pressure near-term margins/billings linearity

DDOG.company_overview: Datadog sells a single SaaS observability and security platform that ingests metrics, traces and logs from a customer's cloud infrastructure and applications, then bills on consumption — per host, per million log events, per span indexed. Roughly 32,700 customers pay it, and 84% of them buy two or more of its ~25 products, which is the entire business model: land on infrastructure monitoring, expand into APM, logs, RUM and now cloud security. It runs a rapid-innovation model, launching a steady stream of differentiated products (Ninja Luxe Cafe espresso, Ninja Crispi, SLUSHi frozen drinks, FlexBreeze fans, CryoGlow beauty masks) that win share from incumbents through feature-led design at accessible price points. FY2025 net sales were $6.4 billion, up 15.7%.

revenue_mix.segment: Beauty & Home Environment (fans, air purifiers, beauty)

moat.type: Rapid product-development engine + dual brand equity + retail shelf presence
moat.narrative: SharkNinja's advantage is speed and cadence of consumer-led innovation: a large in-house engineering organization that ships category-redefining products (SLUSHi, Ninja Crispi, CryoGlow) faster than incumbents, backed by two trusted mass-market brands (Shark, Ninja) and strong big-box and Amazon shelf placement. The moat is execution and brand momentum rather than patents; it must keep out-innovating to defend it, but the launch machine and international runway make share gains durable.

key_customers: Big-box and e-commerce retail channels (Walmart, Target, Amazon, Costco) plus direct-to-consumer; sells to end consumers, retailer concentration typical of the category
key_risks: Reliance on a continuous hit-product pipeline — any innovation slowdown compresses growth
China-centric manufacturing base exposed to US tariffs and supply-chain shifts
Intense competition from Dyson, De'Longhi and low-cost entrants
Retailer inventory and promotional dynamics (Walmart/Amazon) pressuring margins
Consumer discretionary demand sensitivity in a weaker macro

PBF.company_overview: PBF Energy is one of the largest independent US petroleum refiners, running six refineries (Delaware City DE, Paulsboro NJ, Toledo OH, Chalmette LA, Torrance CA and Martinez CA) with about 1.0 million barrels/day of capacity and a high weighted-average Nelson Complexity of ~12.8. It buys crude oil, refines it into gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and other products, and sells them wholesale; it also owns supporting logistics assets and a 50% stake in St. Bernard Renewables, a renewable-diesel joint venture with Eni.

revenue_mix.segment: Renewable diesel (St. Bernard Renewables 50% JV, equity-accounted)

geo_mix.region: US only — East Coast refining (Delaware City, Paulsboro), throughput share

The 'moat' is execution, complexity capture and location, not a defensible franchise.

key_customers: Wholesale and commercial buyers of refined products via spot and term contracts (marketers, distributors, airlines, other refiners); no single dominant customer

RAND.AS.company_overview: Randstad is the world's largest staffing and workforce-solutions company, placing temporary and permanent workers and running outsourced hiring programs across roughly 39 markets. Following a 2024-25 reorganization it sells through four specializations: Operational (light industrial, logistics, skilled trades, commercial), Professional (accounting, office, management), Digital (Randstad Digital: cloud, data, engineering) and Enterprise (large MSP/RPO accounts). FY2025 revenue was about EUR 23.1 billion; the Netherlands, France, Germany and the US are its key markets.

geo_mix.region: Europe (France, Netherlands, Germany, Iberia, Italy, Belgium) approx
Rest of world (Japan, Asia-Pacific, Latin America) approx

moat.type: Scale and local density in home markets — structurally thin, cyclical

Its advantages are being the global scale leader, deep local branch density and brand strength in home markets (Netherlands, France, Belgium), technology investment (Randstad Digital, AI matching) and embedded MSP/RPO relationships that raise switching costs for large enterprise clients. FX translation across many currencies

EDEN.PA.company_overview: Edenred is a global B2B payments and prepaid-voucher company. Employers pay it to issue tax-advantaged meal and food vouchers, employee-benefit cards, corporate mobility/fleet fuel cards and B2B corporate-payment solutions; employees and drivers redeem these at a network of affiliated merchants. Edenred makes money on commissions charged to clients, fees from merchants, and float income earned on prepaid balances held between issuance and redemption. FY2025 operating revenue was EUR 2,732 million, up 6.2% like-for-like.

geo_mix.region: Europe (France ~12% of group, Italy, Iberia, Germany)
Latin America (Brazil the largest single country)
Rest of world (North America, Asia, MEA)

As essentially a global duopoly with Pluxee in meal vouchers, it also earns interest 'float' on prepaid balances and is deepening lock-in via the shift from paper vouchers to cards and apps — a genuinely strong moat.

Competition from Pluxee and fast-growing digital challenger Swile

ZBRA.company_overview: Zebra makes the hardware and software frontline workers use to track and move goods: rugged mobile computers, barcode scanners, RFID readers and tags, industrial/label printers and supplies, plus machine vision and workflow software. It digitizes warehouses, stores, factories and hospitals through combined devices-plus-software 'asset intelligence' solutions. FY2025 revenue was $5.396 billion, up 8.3%. revenue_mix.segment: Connected Frontline / CF (mobile computing, data capture/scanners, RFID)
Asset Visibility & Automation / AVA (printing, supplies, machine vision, robotics)

NWL.company_overview: Consumer products conglomerate selling everyday household brands - Rubbermaid (food storage/commercial), Sharpie and Paper Mate (writing), Graco and NUK (baby gear), Yankee Candle, Coleman (camping), Crock-Pot, Oster and Mr. Coffee (small appliances) - primarily through mass retailers like Walmart, Amazon and Target. revenue_mix.segment: Home & Commercial Solutions (Rubbermaid, Yankee Candle, appliances)

W.company_overview: Pure-play online retailer of furniture and home goods (Wayfair.com plus AllModern, Birch Lane, Joss & Main, Perigold, and B2B arm Wayfair Professional). CRL.company_overview: The world's largest contract provider of preclinical drug-development services and lab animals. KLR.L.company_overview: The world's largest geotechnical specialist contractor - it prepares and stabilises the ground beneath construction projects using ground improvement, piling, grouting and earth-retention techniques so buildings, bridges, data centres, ports and industrial plants can be built on difficult soils. Power, LNG and renewables civil works

HALO.company_overview: Halozyme is a royalty machine, not a drug company. Its enzyme rHuPH20 temporarily breaks down hyaluronan under the skin, letting large-volume biologics be injected subcutaneously in minutes instead of infused for hours. It licenses that technology — branded ENHANZE — to big pharma, which reformulates blockbusters as subcutaneous versions and pays Halozyme royalties on the resulting sales. Ten ENHANZE products are commercial in 100+ markets. Halozyme also sells two proprietary products (Hylenex, XYOSTED), supplies bulk rHuPH20, and has bought two hyperconcentration platforms (Hypercon from Elektrofi, and Surf Bio). FY2025 revenue was $1,396.6m; 2026 guidance was raised to $1.835-1.910bn.

moat.type: Contractual royalty annuities on other people's blockbusters, protected by a layered patent estate
moat.narrative: Once a partner reformulates a $10bn drug with rHuPH20, runs the bridging trials and gets it approved, that molecule is co-formulated with Halozyme's enzyme for the rest of its commercial life — switching would require a new BLA and new clinical data, which no sponsor will do for a marketed product. That is why royalties compound at 40-50% with essentially no incremental cost to Halozyme. The real question is patent runway rather than switching cost: core rHuPH20 composition claims run to roughly 2027, so durability depends on later-filed coformulation and manufacturing patents (the MDASE family Halozyme is asserting against Merck) and on contractual royalty terms. Management is buying its way past that cliff with Hypercon and Surf Bio, which extend the royalty opportunity toward the mid-2040s but do not produce revenue until the first projected launches in 2030-31.

WEX.company_overview: WEX issues and processes closed-loop payment cards and virtual cards for three unrelated buyer groups: commercial vehicle fleets buying fuel, employers administering tax-advantaged health accounts (HSA/FSA/COBRA), and corporates paying suppliers (heavily online travel agencies). It earns interchange on transaction value, per-account/per-vehicle servicing fees, finance charges on late-paying fleets, and interest on the ~$4.2bn of HSA cash deposited at its own industrial bank, WEX Bank.

MANH.company_overview: Manhattan Associates writes and sells the software that runs warehouses, store fulfilment and order management for large retailers, wholesalers, manufacturers and 3PLs. Its Manhattan Active suite is delivered as a versionless, multi-tenant SaaS subscription on five-year-plus contracts, and roughly half of revenue comes from the implementation consulting needed to deploy it. Cash-generative, no debt, $328.7m cash and investments at end-2025.
end_markets: Specialty and department-store retail (omnichannel order management, store fulfilment)
Grocery and consumer packaged goods distribution
top_competitors: Blue Yonder / Panasonic (formerly JDA) — the closest direct WMS rival
Oracle (WMS Cloud, NetSuite, and Oracle POS)
Aptos, Jumpmind, Salesforce (in point-of-sale / order management)
In-house engineering teams at the largest retailers (Amazon-style build-not-buy)

moat.type: Mission-critical embedded system + multi-year contracted backlog + implementation ecosystem
moat.narrative: A WMS is the operational nervous system of a distribution centre — ripping it out means re-training thousands of pickers, re-integrating conveyors and robotics, and risking the fulfilment peak, so replacement cycles run 10-20 years and incumbents almost never lose renewals. That shows up as $2.2bn of remaining performance obligations at end-2025 (up 25% YoY), of which over 98% is non-cancellable cloud subscription with terms longer than a year. The versionless single-codebase architecture of Manhattan Active is genuinely differentiated — customers get quarterly innovation with zero-downtime updates rather than the multi-year upgrade projects that plague SAP EWM and legacy Blue Yonder estates. Risk to the moat is not displacement but deal-cycle elongation: services revenue fell from $525.5m to $503.0m in 2025 as customers slowed new implementations.

REP.MC.company_overview: Repsol is a Spanish integrated energy company. It produces oil and gas (548 kboe/d average in 2025, roughly two-thirds gas), refines over 1 million barrels per day across six refineries in Spain and Peru, and sells the output through more than 4,500 service stations — 3,270 of them in Spain — plus retail electricity, gas and LPG contracts. It is unusual among European majors in that the customer-facing energy retail business, not upstream, is its fastest-growing profit pool.

revenue_mix.segment: Upstream (E&P) — share of FY25 segment adjusted net income, €957m
Customer (mobility, LPG, power & gas retail, aviation, lubricants) — €754m

end_markets: Iberian road fuel retail and EV charging (Waylet app)
Spanish and Portuguese household/SME electricity and gas supply
Aviation fuel and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF)
LNG and natural gas sales into North American and European markets
top_competitors: Moeve (formerly Cepsa) and BP/Shell in Iberian fuel retail
Iberdrola, Endesa and Naturgy in Spanish power and gas retail
TotalEnergies and Eni among European integrated peers in renewables and biofuels
Neste in renewable diesel/HVO and SAF

moat.narrative: Repsol owns the only integrated refining-to-forecourt chain of scale in Spain: six refineries feeding 3,270 domestic service stations, which no competitor can replicate because new refining and forecourt permitting in Spain is effectively closed. That physical position is being converted into a multi-energy customer relationship — bundling fuel, electricity, gas and EV charging to the same household through the Waylet app — which is why Customer adjusted net income rose 17% to €754m in a year when both Upstream and Industrial fell. The upstream book, by contrast, has no structural moat: it is a mid-tier, gas-weighted portfolio competing on cost, and Repsol has already sold 25% of Repsol Upstream Solutions to EIG. BME.L.company_overview: B&M is a UK limited-assortment discount variety retailer. It sells around 6,000 SKUs of branded groceries and general merchandise from out-of-town, low-rent, no-frills stores with no e-commerce channel at all, buying opportunistically and direct from Asia to undercut supermarkets. The group runs three fascias: B&M UK (799 stores), Heron Foods/B&M Express convenience (342 stores) and B&M France (147 stores at FY26 year-end, 28 March 2026).

moat.type: Cost-to-serve advantage — thin, and currently impaired

That model historically supported double-digit EBITDA margins. SHC.company_overview: Sotera Health is an outsourced sterilization and lab-testing utility for the medical device and pharma industry. Sterigenics runs 48 sterilization plants in 13 countries using ethylene oxide, gamma and X-ray; Nordion is the world's leading supplier of Cobalt-60, the isotope that gamma sterilization consumes; Nelson Labs does the microbiological and analytical testing that validates those processes. Revenue is fee-per-unit-processed under multi-year contracts, and 2025 was its 20th consecutive year of revenue growth.
end_markets: Single-use medical devices (syringes, catheters, implants, surgical kits) — the dominant end market
Pharmaceutical and biologics packaging and components
Oncology radiotherapy equipment (high-specific-activity Co-60 for Gamma Knife stereotactic radiosurgery)
Food safety irradiation and agricultural products
Advanced materials — power semiconductors, polymer cross-linking, gemstones
top_competitors: STERIS plc (Applied Sterilization Technologies segment) — the only comparable global outsourced sterilizer
In-house sterilization capacity built by large device OEMs
Regional/niche contract sterilizers and E-beam service providers
Domestic Co-60 producers in Russia, Argentina and India (Nordion's only real isotope competition)
Eurofins, SGS, Charles River and regional labs in Nelson Labs' testing market

moat.type: Regulatory lock-in on validated processes + physical network + isotope scarcity
moat.narrative: Once a device manufacturer validates a sterilization process at a specific Sterigenics facility, that facility is written into the FDA submission — moving it requires re-validation and a regulatory filing, which is why Sterigenics has renewed 100% of its top-ten customers for more than five consecutive years and averages over a decade of tenure with its top 25. Over 90% of Sterigenics revenue and roughly 90% of Nordion revenue sits under multi-year contracts. Physical replication is prohibitive: a new facility costs over $50m plus multi-year licensing, and EO permitting in the US has become effectively impossible post-litigation. Nordion is arguably the harder moat still — Co-60 is produced in a handful of CANDU-type reactors, and gamma accounts for roughly 30% of global single-use device sterilization, so Nordion sells to Sterigenics and to Sterigenics' competitors alike.

key_customers: Sterigenics serves more than 2,000 customers; Nelson Labs approximately 3,000 — no single customer exceeded 10% of total revenue
Global medical device OEMs and their contract manufacturers, served at multiple facilities each
Outsourced contract sterilizers (including Sterigenics itself) and in-house device sterilizers buying Nordion Co-60
Manufacturers of Gamma Knife and other stereotactic radiosurgery systems requiring high-specific-activity Co-60
key_risks: Ethylene oxide tort litigation is the defining risk: a 2022 Cook County verdict produced a $358.7m judgment, followed by a $408.0m settlement of 880+ Willowbrook claims (2023), $30.9m for 97 claims (finalised Sept 2025) and $34.0m for 129 more (July 2025) — the settlement drumbeat has not stopped, and Georgia property-devaluation and personal-injury cases remain pending
Nelson Labs revenue declined 3.9% in 2025 — the only segment shrinking, and the one most exposed to device-industry R&D budgets
Cobalt-60 supply depends on a small set of nuclear reactors; Russian sanctions (in either direction) and reactor outage schedules could disrupt Nordion's feedstock

In the United States there is a single commercial supplier of ethylene oxide to the sterilization industry — a genuine single point of failure, only partially mitigated by Sotera's own EO distribution licence
EPA and state-level EO emissions rules keep tightening, forcing capital spend on emissions control and constraining capacity at existing sites
Customers building in-house sterilization capacity, and the gradual shift from EO/gamma toward X-ray, could erode the installed-base lock-in over a decade

HRB.company_overview: H&R Block prepares tax returns for consumers and small businesses, filing 22.3 million returns by or through the company in fiscal 2026 (year ended 30 June 2026). Roughly two-thirds of revenue is assisted preparation in company-owned and franchised offices; the rest is DIY software, franchise royalties, and attached financial products — Refund Transfers, the Emerald Card, Spruce mobile banking and Emerald Advance loans — plus Wave, a small-business accounting and payments platform.

International consumer tax markets — Canada, Australia, Brazil, India

moat.type: Physical distribution to the refund-driven filer + regulatory complexity — a slowly eroding moat
moat.narrative: The real asset is a nationwide office network reaching a customer who wants a human, a same-day advance against their refund, and a guarantee — a bundle Intuit cannot fully replicate remotely. That bundling is why net average charge keeps rising even as return volumes stagnate, and why financial products (Refund Transfers, Emerald Advance, Refund Advance) attach so profitably: they monetise the refund, not the return. Regulatory complexity is the second leg — every tax code change re-creates demand for help. But be honest about direction: DIY revenue grew 0.2% in fiscal 2026 and Intuit's TurboTax Live is attacking the assisted segment from the low-cost side. Management is offsetting the flat top line with buybacks, shrinking diluted shares from 137.3m to 128.9m in one year, which flatters EPS more than it widens the moat.

Franchisees operating under the H&R Block brand, contributing $185.4m of royalties
Pathward, N.A. as the issuing bank partner for Emerald Card, Spruce and refund-related lending products
Wave's small-business subscriber base — second consecutive year of double-digit revenue growth
